BREWMASTER STAGGER EXPLAINED
On top of being able to frequently dodge enemy attacks with  Mastery: Elusive Brawler, Brewmaster Monks are the only specialization featuring the additional mechanic of  Stagger to further mitigate damage. With this passive effect, all damage you receive will be split into two portions:
An instant portion - immediately damaging you like any attack normally does.
A  Staggered portion - dealing damage to you every 0.5 seconds, for a total of 10 seconds. With the  Bob and Weave talent, this is extended to 15 seconds instead.
The amount of Physical damage you can delay taking with  Stagger is mostly based upon how much Agility you have. From there, only 58% of that value will apply to any magical damage (including most damage-over-time debuffs). While you are Staggering damage, you will also receive one of three debuffs based upon how much damage you are taking compared to your maximum health:
 Light Stagger (Green) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 1-29% of your maximum health.
 Moderate Stagger (Yellow) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 30-59% of your maximum health.
 Heavy Stagger (Red) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 60% or more of your maximum health.
Note that although there are only these three debuffs, you may regularly reach periods of  Staggering 100% or more of your health in harder content! As such, you do not always need to be worried about reaching  Heavy Stagger, so long as you are receiving a steady amount of healing to offset the damage.
Of course, simply taking the same amount of damage over a longer period of time does not mean you've actually mitigated or reduced the amount taken. This is where your other main mitigation ability of  Purifying Brew comes in. This ability has a 20-second recharge time and two charges. When used, you will instantly Purify 50% of the total amount of damage you are currently  Staggering. An example of how this all works out is like so:
Assume you have a  Stagger amount of 50% against Physical damage.
You are hit for 25,000 damage by an enemy. Thanks to  Stagger, this damage is split.
You instantly take 12,500 damage.
The other 12,500 damage enters your  Stagger pool.
You are now taking 625 damage every 0.5 seconds from  Stagger, gradually depleting your Stagger pool. After 10 seconds, you will have taken another 12,500 total damage.
With the  Bob and Weave talent extending the duration of  Stagger to 15 seconds, this would instead be ~417 damage every 0.5 seconds!
After 5 seconds, you cast  Purifying Brew, which removes 50% of your current  Stagger pool. At this point, you still had 6,250 damage left to take, so 3,125 damage is now Purified.
After 10 total seconds have passed, you suffered 12,500 instant damage, and only 9,375 in  Stagger damage. By using  Purifying Brew, you have taken 3,125 less damage from that original hit of 25,000!
If you had used  Purifying Brew a little faster, such as after only 1 second, you would've taken 5,625 less damage instead. Purifying earlier will prevent more damage!

GIFT/SPIRIT OF THE OX HEALING SPHERES
Your  Gift of the Ox passive is one that has a very misleading effect. While it may claim to only have a chance to summon its  Healing Spheres, this ability is instead entirely predictable. This is because it follows a consistent rule: you will generate one Healing Sphere every time you have taken 100% of your maximum health as damage. While this may seem like a daunting amount of damage, it is actually calculated from the "raw" damage values hitting you (after any damage reductions such as Armor or a cooldown like  Fortifying Brew), before they are reduced by your own  Stagger passive or absorb effects.

Once they have appeared, your  Healing Spheres will linger on the battlefield for up to 30 seconds before automatically being consumed. However, you may only have up to 5 orbs active at a time, and notably, all Healing Spheres behave this way whether they are spawned by  Gift of the Ox or  Spirit of the Ox. If any further spawns occur beyond this point, the oldest of your orbs will be automatically consumed and heal you to stay at this cap.

If the thought of having to look for your  Healing Spheres when you want extra healing is annoying, fortunately there is a reliable alternative in the form of the  Expel Harm spell. This ability, which costs 15 Energy and has a 5-second cooldown, will heal you for a small baseline amount in addition to consuming all active Healing Spheres. It will even deal damage equal to 10% of the total amount of healing done (including overhealing) to your active target afterward. Notably, when consuming Healing Spheres this way, they will also have their healing buffed by the  Strength of Spirit talent.
Overall,  Healing Spheres from  Gift of the Ox and  Spirit of the Ox represent your biggest form of self-healing. Thanks to  Expel Harm and the  Strength of Spirit talent—not to mention the  Celestial Fortune passive—it is not uncommon to fully heal yourself off of only one or two orbs at lower health. You should still try to be mindful of how many are present at once and judge whether or not you need to consume them all, however. Likewise, due to  Spinning Crane Kick passively dragging any active Healing Spheres toward your location, you may inadvertently consume some. Keep track of this total by watching the number on your  Expel Harm ability.

EXPLODING KEG‎
 Exploding Keg is your shortest damage cooldown as a Brewmaster, and like most abilities in your kit, it also has some built-in defensive benefits. Once every minute, you may use this ability to deal the largest amount of burst damage available to you. This makes it an excellent option early on in a pull against many enemies for establishing threat while also resetting the cooldown on  Keg Smash to potentially follow up with even more. As an added bonus, it also brings defensive perks, making enemy melee attacks deal only a single point of damage for a brief moment. However, this reduction to enemy melee attacks is largely ignorable, as it only applies to auto attacks. In addition, if these attacks are also meant to apply a debuff upon successfully hitting their target, you will still receive them despite being hit for only 1 damage. You are not necessarily safe.

Beyond its reliable burst of Fire damage and  Keg Smash reset, any enemies debuffed to deal reduced damage to you will also receive small amounts of bonus Fire damage if damaged by anything in your kit. This includes abilities that hit multiple times, such as the ticks of  Rushing Jade Wind,  Spinning Crane Kick, or a Shado-Pan Brewmaster's  Flurry Strikes. In theory, this means you can take advantage of these short windows for a further damage buff.

So, with this in mind, what is the best use of  Exploding Keg? Unfortunately, as exciting as it sounds to follow up each cast of the ability with a couple  Spinning Crane Kick, the small bits of Fire damage do not make up for using stronger abilities instead, and will usually in a damage loss. The main exceptions to this are exceptionally large pulls or when fighting enemies that won't be alive for much longer. Instead, focus on having  Rushing Jade Wind active beforehand (if talented), and simply continuing your normal rotation priority. If you are using the Shado-Pan Hero Talents, trying to cast a  Keg Smash to trigger  Flurry Strikes is a good idea too. Don't forget that your Keg Smash can also potentially trigger  Fuel on the Fire, and you can also cast  Empty the Cellar, if either are talented!

OPTIMIZING BLACKOUT COMBO
Due to adding effects to some of your core rotational abilities,  Blackout Combo is a talent that is important to play around effectively. This begins with continuing to prioritize the use of  Blackout Kick on cooldown, so you may empower as many abilities as possible. However, this results in the talent being a difficult option to play optimally.

When taking on  Blackout Combo, the choice of what ability to empower is usually a simple one. In most circumstances, you will all but exclusively consume the buffs provided by your  Blackout Kicks on  Tiger Palm to give it bonus damage. This is particularly useful due to Tiger Palm already having a number of additional damage modifiers in talents, such as  Counterstrike,  Face Palm, and a Master of Harmony's  Meditative Focus, enabling it to greatly exceed its regular potential. Due to this,  Keg Smash should rarely be comboed for its extra cooldown reduction, or this talent will lose most of its value due to the lost damage relative to the minor defensive gain.

Of course, with  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm being two of your most frequently-pressed abilities, the biggest key to you empowering the abilities you want with  Blackout Combo is to take advantage of abilities that do not have a combo effect. If they are used instead, you will keep your Blackout Combo buff and may still use it on another ability later. All of your other main abilities are fair game for this, such as  Breath of Fire,  Spinning Crane Kick,  Rushing Jade Wind,  Chi Burst, alongside all of your cooldowns and defensive abilities. By making good use of these "gap-filling" abilities, you can still reliably consume every  Blackout Kick's buff with Tiger Palm instead of Keg Smash. Don't forget about it!

Pre-Combat Checks.content:
PRE-COMBAT CHECK
For the most part, a Brewmaster does not have much to worry about before starting a pull; all of your buffs and debuffs will be applied within the first ability or two of your rotation, such as  Shuffle and  Mystic Touch. Nevertheless, here are some universal things to especially watch for in raids or dungeons, but can also apply to delves or even open-world content:

Consumables Check - If planning to use them, ensure your flask, food, weapon enhancement, and optional augment rune buffs will last for the duration of combat. By default, each lasts for the following length of time:
Flask - 1 hour (2 for Alchemists);
Food - 1 hour (removed on death if not consuming "hearty" food);
Weapon enhancement - 2 hours;
Augment Rune - 1 hour (removed on death).

As a Brewmaster Monk, your goal as a tank will be to maintain 100% uptime on your  Shuffle passive, while then finding the best times to make use of  Purifying Brew and  Celestial Brew or  Celestial Infusion. While their base cooldowns are long, they, along with any other ability with "Brew" in the name, will gain cooldown reduction. Your  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm will provide 3 seconds and 1 second of reduction, respectively, with every cast. This results in effectively halving the base cooldowns of your Brews.

Once you have begun using your abilities and built up  Shuffle, it is time to start thinking about when to use  Purifying Brew. To keep things simple, here are three basic rules you can follow:
Avoid having both charges of  Purifying Brew sitting off cooldown. You are wasting cooldown reduction if you do!
Make use of a charge right after taking a big spike of damage. This maximizes the amount of damage Purified from your  Stagger pool.
Use a charge if the second one is about to come off cooldown.
For the most part, if you are following these rules you will likely be acting as if  Purifying Brew only has one charge available at any given time. With how frequently your charges of it regenerate, this is fine, and has the benefit of giving you an extra cushion against multiple large hits in a row. It may also mean, however, that you will need to occasionally use Purifying Brew while only having  Moderate Stagger or even  Light Stagger. So long as you still have that extra charge for when damage spikes occur, that's what will matter most.

Brewmaster Monks are somewhat unique among tanks in that they can choose between two similar mitigation abilities:  Celestial Brew and  Celestial Infusion. Each of these options have moments where one may be better than the other, and this choice is also closely intertwined with the  Niuzao's Resolve talent (discussed further below).

 Celestial Brew is a traditional defensive tool, generating a large damage absorbing shield for up to 8 seconds or until its damage cap has been reached. This shield can allow you to handle dangerous mechanics all on its own without needing to use another, longer defensive cooldown. However, it is prone to wasting much of the passive healing a Brewmaster receives while it is active. After all, if you were to reach full health with the absorb still present against oncoming damage, then all of the mitigation is being spent in that moment and leaving you just as vulnerable when it expires, possibly giving your healers a false sense of security until your health suddenly drops again.

This is where the alternate choice of  Celestial Infusion comes in. Although its shield size and cooldown are the same, this ability instead only absorbs a portion of the damage you receive for up to 16 seconds or until its cap is reached. To think of it another way, you are gaining a 30% damage reduction to a point, compared to 100% damage reduction for a shorter time from  Celestial Brew. By having a smaller amount of mitigation spread out over a longer period of time, you become easier to heal overall by reducing the "spikiness" that comes from an "all or nothing" type of defense. Plus, while the amount absorbed from a given hit is smaller, your own  Stagger and other mitigating abilities rarely makes this any deadlier.

So, where does this leave the decision between these two Brew abilities? In general, most players will have a better Brewmaster experience by defaulting to  Celestial Infusion in the majority of content, especially in combination with  Niuzao's Resolve. It will not create as many opportunities to make mistakes, but there is a limit to how useful this setup can be. If you are going up against more overwhelming sources of spikey damage, then the shorter and stronger reduction of  Celestial Brew may be just what you need. Similarly, those moments are also when you may wish to consider dropping Niuzao's Resolve in favor of more traditional healing through  Expel Harm.

AWAKENING SPIRIT VS VITAL FLAME 
One of your most frequent defensive talent choices (when necessary) will be between  Awakening Spirit and  Vital Flame. Both have their pros and cons.
 Awakening Spirit applies a shield whenever you cast  Purifying Brew that specifically only absorbs damage from the  Stagger DoT. This shield's size will be the same regardless of your Stagger level when casting Purifying Brew, and its buff will not stack if casting the ability twice in quick succession. It is important to note that this absorb shield is relatively small compared to your maximum health (usually less than 5% of it), but this means it can be easily consumed in any content where you are properly making use of Purifying Brew!
 Vital Flame, meanwhile, is another passive effect that causes you to heal for 50% of your Nature and Fire damage dealt by abilities. For the most part, this does work as described. There are a few notable exceptions, such as  Fuel on the Fire, which does not activate this healing when it should, but it is otherwise a consistent source of self-healing.
Despite the odd ability effects that do not properly interact, the choice between these two talents is easy enough: default to  Awakening Spirit in single-target combat and  Vital Flame in AoE content where more enemies are being damaged by your abilities. Both are a small enough part of your overall mitigation to allow you to use either of them anywhere, but it's good to get into the habit of customizing your defenses to the situation.

 Fortifying Brew is your most powerful defensive cooldown on a Brewmaster Monk, offering a temporary increase to your health in addition to a flat damage reduction and a guaranteed Empty Barrel from  Bring Me Another for added bonuses. You can further enhance its strength with talents such as  Ironshell Brew or  Fortifying Brew: Determination, bumping the health and mitigation or having it also buff your ability to  Stagger damage while active. Unfortunately, this incredibly powerful cooldown (when combined with the natural sturdiness a Brewmaster already has) is offset by an equally incredible cooldown time of 6 minutes.

While a 6-minute cooldown may seem like a dealbreaker,  Fortifying Brew does have "Brew" in its name, which means that it benefits from the cooldown reduction effects of both  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm. In total, this means that this lengthy duration is roughly cut in half when actively fighting and properly performing your rotation. If you are desperate enough to need it even more frequently for whatever reason, you may also opt into reducing its baseline cooldown by 2 minutes with the  Expeditious Fortification talent, though this will keep you from having the bonus health and reduction of  Ironshell Brew.

With this cooldown secretly being a 2-3 minute ability in disguise, it becomes a much more flexible choice for defense. In general, you should aim to use it proactively, before you have dropped to dangerously low health. Of course, since it offers both damage reduction and additional health it can still be used reactively for a greater benefit than many other defensive buttons. If you don't need its defense at all, you may even consider activating it purely for the health increase to buff the damage of  Touch of Death. So long as you are using the ability at all, it is acting as a more effective defensive than sitting around being concerned about its ominous recharge time.

CHARRED PASSIONS VS DRAGONFIRE BREW 
With  Charred Passions, your  Blackout Kicks in particular become especially powerful for a short time after casting  Breath of Fire. Thanks to the  Sal'salabim's Strength talent (recommended in all Brewmaster builds), this short time will actually be at all times instead, resulting in Charred Passions being a noteworthy buff to your damage in smaller pulls. While it may also apply its damage buff to your  Spinning Crane Kick, you often will not have space in the rotation to be casting it repeatedly, especially if you have also talented into  Blackout Combo. Likewise, your performance with this talent will suffer if you do not reliably press Blackout Kick on cooldown.
 Dragonfire Brew acts as an even more passive alternative, increasing your  Breath of Fire damage and breathing two additional times. Due to Breath of Fire's more generous AoE scaling, this talent offers more damage in larger pulls. Notably, this additional upfront Fire damage also interacts well with the  Vital Flame talent.
Overall, the choice between these two talents becomes somewhat of a matter of preference. While  Charred Passions offers better performance in strictly single or low-target fights,  Dragonfire Brew can still keep up and gain a noteworthy advantage in larger pulls without even relying on the pressure of you needing to be the best at pressing  Blackout Kick on cooldown.
 ADDENDUM: CHARRED PASSIONS AND SCALDING BREW
If  Scalding Brew is talented into rather than  Sal'salabim's Strength, then you are no longer able to maintain  Breath of Fire's DoT effect by itself due to the debuff lasting for a few seconds less than the ability's cooldown. Fortunately,  Charred Passions is also able to refresh this debuff's duration every time you cast  Blackout Kick or  Spinning Crane Kick while empowered by its effect after casting Breath of Fire, which also means you will always benefit from Scalding Brew's bonus damage.

However, because of this interaction you must always talent into  Charred Passions if using  Scalding Brew;  Dragonfire Brew is no longer an option.

 Further Details

BREWMASTER STAGGER EXPLAINED
On top of being able to frequently dodge enemy attacks with  Mastery: Elusive Brawler, Brewmaster Monks are the only specialization featuring the additional mechanic of  Stagger to further mitigate damage. With this passive effect, all damage you receive will be split into two portions:
An instant portion - immediately damaging you like any attack normally does.
A  Staggered portion - dealing damage to you every 0.5 seconds, for a total of 10 seconds. With the  Bob and Weave talent, this is extended to 15 seconds instead.
The amount of Physical damage you can delay taking with  Stagger is mostly based upon how much Agility you have. From there, only 58% of that value will apply to any magical damage (including most damage-over-time debuffs). While you are Staggering damage, you will also receive one of three debuffs based upon how much damage you are taking compared to your maximum health:
 Light Stagger (Green) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 1-29% of your maximum health.
 Moderate Stagger (Yellow) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 30-59% of your maximum health.
 Heavy Stagger (Red) - Your total amount of  Staggered damage is equal to 60% or more of your maximum health.
Note that although there are only these three debuffs, you may regularly reach periods of  Staggering 100% or more of your health in harder content! As such, you do not always need to be worried about reaching  Heavy Stagger, so long as you are receiving a steady amount of healing to offset the damage.
Of course, simply taking the same amount of damage over a longer period of time does not mean you've actually mitigated or reduced the amount taken. This is where your other main mitigation ability of  Purifying Brew comes in. This ability has a 20-second recharge time and two charges. When used, you will instantly Purify 50% of the total amount of damage you are currently  Staggering. An example of how this all works out is like so:
Assume you have a  Stagger amount of 50% against Physical damage.
You are hit for 25,000 damage by an enemy. Thanks to  Stagger, this damage is split.
You instantly take 12,500 damage.
The other 12,500 damage enters your  Stagger pool.
You are now taking 625 damage every 0.5 seconds from  Stagger, gradually depleting your Stagger pool. After 10 seconds, you will have taken another 12,500 total damage.
With the  Bob and Weave talent extending the duration of  Stagger to 15 seconds, this would instead be ~417 damage every 0.5 seconds!
After 5 seconds, you cast  Purifying Brew, which removes 50% of your current  Stagger pool. At this point, you still had 6,250 damage left to take, so 3,125 damage is now Purified.
After 10 total seconds have passed, you suffered 12,500 instant damage, and only 9,375 in  Stagger damage. By using  Purifying Brew, you have taken 3,125 less damage from that original hit of 25,000!
If you had used  Purifying Brew a little faster, such as after only 1 second, you would've taken 5,625 less damage instead. Purifying earlier will prevent more damage!
 Full Stagger Formula

GIFT/SPIRIT OF THE OX HEALING SPHERES
Your  Gift of the Ox passive is one that has a very misleading effect. While it may claim to only have a chance to summon its  Healing Spheres, this ability is instead entirely predictable. This is because it follows a consistent rule: you will generate one Healing Sphere every time you have taken 100% of your maximum health as damage. While this may seem like a daunting amount of damage, it is actually calculated from the "raw" damage values hitting you (after any damage reductions such as Armor or a cooldown like  Fortifying Brew), before they are reduced by your own  Stagger passive or absorb effects.

Once they have appeared, your  Healing Spheres will linger on the battlefield for up to 30 seconds before automatically being consumed. However, you may only have up to 5 orbs active at a time, and notably, all Healing Spheres behave this way whether they are spawned by  Gift of the Ox or  Spirit of the Ox. If any further spawns occur beyond this point, the oldest of your orbs will be automatically consumed and heal you to stay at this cap.

If the thought of having to look for your  Healing Spheres when you want extra healing is annoying, fortunately there is a reliable alternative in the form of the  Expel Harm spell. This ability, which costs 15 Energy and has a 5-second cooldown, will heal you for a small baseline amount in addition to consuming all active Healing Spheres. It will even deal damage equal to 10% of the total amount of healing done (including overhealing) to your active target afterward. Notably, when consuming Healing Spheres this way, they will also have their healing buffed by the  Strength of Spirit talent.
Overall,  Healing Spheres from  Gift of the Ox and  Spirit of the Ox represent your biggest form of self-healing. Thanks to  Expel Harm and the  Strength of Spirit talent—not to mention the  Celestial Fortune passive—it is not uncommon to fully heal yourself off of only one or two orbs at lower health. You should still try to be mindful of how many are present at once and judge whether or not you need to consume them all, however. Likewise, due to  Spinning Crane Kick passively dragging any active Healing Spheres toward your location, you may inadvertently consume some. Keep track of this total by watching the number on your  Expel Harm ability.

EXPLODING KEG‎
 Exploding Keg is your shortest damage cooldown as a Brewmaster, and like most abilities in your kit, it also has some built-in defensive benefits. Once every minute, you may use this ability to deal the largest amount of burst damage available to you. This makes it an excellent option early on in a pull against many enemies for establishing threat while also resetting the cooldown on  Keg Smash to potentially follow up with even more. As an added bonus, it also brings defensive perks, making enemy melee attacks deal only a single point of damage for a brief moment. However, this reduction to enemy melee attacks is largely ignorable, as it only applies to auto attacks. In addition, if these attacks are also meant to apply a debuff upon successfully hitting their target, you will still receive them despite being hit for only 1 damage. You are not necessarily safe.

Beyond its reliable burst of Fire damage and  Keg Smash reset, any enemies debuffed to deal reduced damage to you will also receive small amounts of bonus Fire damage if damaged by anything in your kit. This includes abilities that hit multiple times, such as the ticks of  Rushing Jade Wind,  Spinning Crane Kick, or a Shado-Pan Brewmaster's  Flurry Strikes. In theory, this means you can take advantage of these short windows for a further damage buff.

So, with this in mind, what is the best use of  Exploding Keg? Unfortunately, as exciting as it sounds to follow up each cast of the ability with a couple  Spinning Crane Kick, the small bits of Fire damage do not make up for using stronger abilities instead, and will usually in a damage loss. The main exceptions to this are exceptionally large pulls or when fighting enemies that won't be alive for much longer. Instead, focus on having  Rushing Jade Wind active beforehand (if talented), and simply continuing your normal rotation priority. If you are using the Shado-Pan Hero Talents, trying to cast a  Keg Smash to trigger  Flurry Strikes is a good idea too. Don't forget that your Keg Smash can also potentially trigger  Fuel on the Fire, and you can also cast  Empty the Cellar, if either are talented!

OPTIMIZING BLACKOUT COMBO
Due to adding effects to some of your core rotational abilities,  Blackout Combo is a talent that is important to play around effectively. This begins with continuing to prioritize the use of  Blackout Kick on cooldown, so you may empower as many abilities as possible. However, this results in the talent being a difficult option to play optimally.

When taking on  Blackout Combo, the choice of what ability to empower is usually a simple one. In most circumstances, you will all but exclusively consume the buffs provided by your  Blackout Kicks on  Tiger Palm to give it bonus damage. This is particularly useful due to Tiger Palm already having a number of additional damage modifiers in talents, such as  Counterstrike,  Face Palm, and a Master of Harmony's  Meditative Focus, enabling it to greatly exceed its regular potential. Due to this,  Keg Smash should rarely be comboed for its extra cooldown reduction, or this talent will lose most of its value due to the lost damage relative to the minor defensive gain.

Of course, with  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm being two of your most frequently-pressed abilities, the biggest key to you empowering the abilities you want with  Blackout Combo is to take advantage of abilities that do not have a combo effect. If they are used instead, you will keep your Blackout Combo buff and may still use it on another ability later. All of your other main abilities are fair game for this, such as  Breath of Fire,  Spinning Crane Kick,  Rushing Jade Wind,  Chi Burst, alongside all of your cooldowns and defensive abilities. By making good use of these "gap-filling" abilities, you can still reliably consume every  Blackout Kick's buff with Tiger Palm instead of Keg Smash. Don't forget about it!

Once every minute, you may use this ability to deal the largest amount of burst damage available to you. This makes it an excellent option early on in a pull against many enemies for establishing threat while also resetting the cooldown on  Keg Smash to potentially follow up with even more. As an added bonus, it also brings defensive perks, making enemy melee attacks deal only a single point of damage for a brief moment. However, this reduction to enemy melee attacks is largely ignorable, as it only applies to auto attacks. In addition, if these attacks are also meant to apply a debuff upon successfully hitting their target, you will still receive them despite being hit for only 1 damage. You are not necessarily safe.

Beyond its reliable burst of Fire damage and  Keg Smash reset, any enemies debuffed to deal reduced damage to you will also receive small amounts of bonus Fire damage if damaged by anything in your kit. This includes abilities that hit multiple times, such as the ticks of  Rushing Jade Wind,  Spinning Crane Kick, or a Shado-Pan Brewmaster's  Flurry Strikes. In theory, this means you can take advantage of these short windows for a further damage buff.

So, with this in mind, what is the best use of  Exploding Keg? Unfortunately, as exciting as it sounds to follow up each cast of the ability with a couple  Spinning Crane Kick, the small bits of Fire damage do not make up for using stronger abilities instead, and will usually in a damage loss. The main exceptions to this are exceptionally large pulls or when fighting enemies that won't be alive for much longer. Don't forget that your Keg Smash can also potentially trigger  Fuel on the Fire, and you can also cast  Empty the Cellar, if either are talented!

Due to adding effects to some of your core rotational abilities,  Blackout Combo is a talent that is important to play around effectively. This begins with continuing to prioritize the use of  Blackout Kick on cooldown, so you may empower as many abilities as possible. However, this results in the talent being a difficult option to play optimally.

When taking on  Blackout Combo, the choice of what ability to empower is usually a simple one. In most circumstances, you will all but exclusively consume the buffs provided by your  Blackout Kicks on  Tiger Palm to give it bonus damage. This is particularly useful due to Tiger Palm already having a number of additional damage modifiers in talents, such as  Counterstrike,  Face Palm, and a Master of Harmony's  Meditative Focus, enabling it to greatly exceed its regular potential. Due to this,  Keg Smash should rarely be comboed for its extra cooldown reduction, or this talent will lose most of its value due to the lost damage relative to the minor defensive gain.

PRE-COMBAT CHECK
For the most part, a Brewmaster does not have much to worry about before starting a pull; all of your buffs and debuffs will be applied within the first ability or two of your rotation, such as  Shuffle and  Mystic Touch. Nevertheless, here are some universal things to especially watch for in raids or dungeons, but can also apply to delves or even open-world content:

Consumables Check - If planning to use them, ensure your flask, food, weapon enhancement, and optional augment rune buffs will last for the duration of combat. By default, each lasts for the following length of time:
Flask - 1 hour (2 for Alchemists);
Food - 1 hour (removed on death if not consuming "hearty" food);
Weapon enhancement - 2 hours;
Augment Rune - 1 hour (removed on death).
Gear Repair - Gear slowly loses durability during combat, and every death will subtract an additional 10% with limited exceptions. Broken gear provides no stats; stay on top of it!
Talent Check - Should you have  Detox or  Pressure Points selected? Look again to be sure.

MANAGING BREWS
As a Brewmaster Monk, your goal as a tank will be to maintain 100% uptime on your  Shuffle passive, while then finding the best times to make use of  Purifying Brew and  Celestial Brew or  Celestial Infusion. While their base cooldowns are long, they, along with any other ability with "Brew" in the name, will gain cooldown reduction. Your  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm will provide 3 seconds and 1 second of reduction, respectively, with every cast. This results in effectively halving the base cooldowns of your Brews.

Once you have begun using your abilities and built up  Shuffle, it is time to start thinking about when to use  Purifying Brew. To keep things simple, here are three basic rules you can follow:
Avoid having both charges of  Purifying Brew sitting off cooldown. You are wasting cooldown reduction if you do!
Make use of a charge right after taking a big spike of damage. This maximizes the amount of damage Purified from your  Stagger pool.
Use a charge if the second one is about to come off cooldown.
For the most part, if you are following these rules you will likely be acting as if  Purifying Brew only has one charge available at any given time. With how frequently your charges of it regenerate, this is fine, and has the benefit of giving you an extra cushion against multiple large hits in a row. It may also mean, however, that you will need to occasionally use Purifying Brew while only having  Moderate Stagger or even  Light Stagger. So long as you still have that extra charge for when damage spikes occur, that's what will matter most.
 CELESTIAL BREW VS CELESTIAL INFUSION 
Brewmaster Monks are somewhat unique among tanks in that they can choose between two similar mitigation abilities:  Celestial Brew and  Celestial Infusion. Each of these options have moments where one may be better than the other, and this choice is also closely intertwined with the  Niuzao's Resolve talent (discussed further below).

 Celestial Brew is a traditional defensive tool, generating a large damage absorbing shield for up to 8 seconds or until its damage cap has been reached. This shield can allow you to handle dangerous mechanics all on its own without needing to use another, longer defensive cooldown. However, it is prone to wasting much of the passive healing a Brewmaster receives while it is active. After all, if you were to reach full health with the absorb still present against oncoming damage, then all of the mitigation is being spent in that moment and leaving you just as vulnerable when it expires, possibly giving your healers a false sense of security until your health suddenly drops again.

This is where the alternate choice of  Celestial Infusion comes in. Although its shield size and cooldown are the same, this ability instead only absorbs a portion of the damage you receive for up to 16 seconds or until its cap is reached. To think of it another way, you are gaining a 30% damage reduction to a point, compared to 100% damage reduction for a shorter time from  Celestial Brew. By having a smaller amount of mitigation spread out over a longer period of time, you become easier to heal overall by reducing the "spikiness" that comes from an "all or nothing" type of defense. Plus, while the amount absorbed from a given hit is smaller, your own  Stagger and other mitigating abilities rarely makes this any deadlier.

So, where does this leave the decision between these two Brew abilities? In general, most players will have a better Brewmaster experience by defaulting to  Celestial Infusion in the majority of content, especially in combination with  Niuzao's Resolve. It will not create as many opportunities to make mistakes, but there is a limit to how useful this setup can be. If you are going up against more overwhelming sources of spikey damage, then the shorter and stronger reduction of  Celestial Brew may be just what you need. Similarly, those moments are also when you may wish to consider dropping Niuzao's Resolve in favor of more traditional healing through  Expel Harm.

AWAKENING SPIRIT VS VITAL FLAME 
One of your most frequent defensive talent choices (when necessary) will be between  Awakening Spirit and  Vital Flame. Both have their pros and cons.
 Awakening Spirit applies a shield whenever you cast  Purifying Brew that specifically only absorbs damage from the  Stagger DoT. This shield's size will be the same regardless of your Stagger level when casting Purifying Brew, and its buff will not stack if casting the ability twice in quick succession. It is important to note that this absorb shield is relatively small compared to your maximum health (usually less than 5% of it), but this means it can be easily consumed in any content where you are properly making use of Purifying Brew!
 Vital Flame, meanwhile, is another passive effect that causes you to heal for 50% of your Nature and Fire damage dealt by abilities. For the most part, this does work as described. There are a few notable exceptions, such as  Fuel on the Fire, which does not activate this healing when it should, but it is otherwise a consistent source of self-healing.
Despite the odd ability effects that do not properly interact, the choice between these two talents is easy enough: default to  Awakening Spirit in single-target combat and  Vital Flame in AoE content where more enemies are being damaged by your abilities. Both are a small enough part of your overall mitigation to allow you to use either of them anywhere, but it's good to get into the habit of customizing your defenses to the situation.

FORTIFYING BREW
 Fortifying Brew is your most powerful defensive cooldown on a Brewmaster Monk, offering a temporary increase to your health in addition to a flat damage reduction and a guaranteed Empty Barrel from  Bring Me Another for added bonuses. You can further enhance its strength with talents such as  Ironshell Brew or  Fortifying Brew: Determination, bumping the health and mitigation or having it also buff your ability to  Stagger damage while active. Unfortunately, this incredibly powerful cooldown (when combined with the natural sturdiness a Brewmaster already has) is offset by an equally incredible cooldown time of 6 minutes.

While a 6-minute cooldown may seem like a dealbreaker,  Fortifying Brew does have "Brew" in its name, which means that it benefits from the cooldown reduction effects of both  Keg Smash and  Tiger Palm. In total, this means that this lengthy duration is roughly cut in half when actively fighting and properly performing your rotation. If you are desperate enough to need it even more frequently for whatever reason, you may also opt into reducing its baseline cooldown by 2 minutes with the  Expeditious Fortification talent, though this will keep you from having the bonus health and reduction of  Ironshell Brew.

With this cooldown secretly being a 2-3 minute ability in disguise, it becomes a much more flexible choice for defense. In general, you should aim to use it proactively, before you have dropped to dangerously low health. Of course, since it offers both damage reduction and additional health it can still be used reactively for a greater benefit than many other defensive buttons. If you don't need its defense at all, you may even consider activating it purely for the health increase to buff the damage of  Touch of Death. So long as you are using the ability at all, it is acting as a more effective defensive than sitting around being concerned about its ominous recharge time.

SHADOWBOXING TREADS VS FLUIDITY OF MOTION 
Arguably the rarest choice node to adjust for a Brewmaster,  Shadowboxing Treads and  Fluidity of Motion both improve your  Blackout Kick ability, though one has a far greater impact on your rotation than the other. For most players, just choose Shadowboxing Treads and use it at all times across every piece of content. Otherwise, those that are willing to take on an even greater challenge can find it here under special circumstances.

 Fluidity of Motion's effect is incredibly simple for its impact: a mere 1-second reduction to the cooldown of  Blackout Kick that brings it down to an ability used every 3 seconds. Where things get exponentially more difficult is when considering how this talent pairs with  Blackout Combo, resulting in two out of every 3 abilities becoming Blackout Kick and  Tiger Palm. This greatly increases the pace of the rotation and adds a hefty Energy cost, while giving you less time to react defensively considering that  Celestial Brew/ Celestial Infusion is also on the global cooldown. Fortunately, this is rarely even a theoretical damage gain. The exception to this rule is when a few conditions are fulfilled:
You are a Master of Harmony Brewmaster
 Black Ox Brew and all four ranks of  Bring Me Another are selected as talents
You are fighting in single-target combat
If you meet these requirements, then  Fluidity of Motion becomes a substantial damage increase thanks to  Bring Me Another and  Black Ox Brew helping to reduce your Energy spent. In particular, this also means that you will no longer cast  Keg Smash unless it is a free Empty Barrel. Should any one condition not be true, then  Shadowboxing Treads remains the superior talent.
